ch26.title: Kabbalah
ch26.summary: The great flowering of Jewish mysticism in medieval Provence and Spain — a map of the hidden God as ten emanations on a Tree of Life, and a universe spoken into being out of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. From the widow of Ávila and the Zohar's true 13th-century authorship (Moses de León, per Scholem, not the 2nd-century sage it names), through the Sefer Yetzirah and the Bahir, Ein Sof and the ten sefirot, the four worlds, the theosophical and the ecstatic (Abulafia) streams, and PaRDeS; with a deep symbology section on the Hebrew letters as the raw material of creation, gematria, notarikon and temurah, and the divine names — keeping attested medieval technique honestly distinct from later Christian Kabbalah, Hermetic Qabalah, and the modern 'Kabbalah Centre.'
ch26.plateCaption: The Tree of Life (Etz Chaim) — the ten sefirot through which the hidden Ein Sof emanates into creation, joined by the twenty-two paths of the Hebrew letters. An original geometric rendering of the traditional figure.

ch27.title: Sufism
ch27.summary: The mystical heart of Islam — a path of love, remembrance, and the annihilation of the self in God. From the whirling sema of the Mevlevi and Rabia's torch-and-bucket to burn heaven and quench hell, through the tasawwuf ascetics and al-Ghazali's great reconciliation of Sufism with orthodox Islam, the high-medieval flowering of Ibn Arabi (wahdat al-wujud) and Rumi's Mathnawi, and the founding of the tariqa orders; with a symbology section on the 99 Names, the wine-and-Beloved code of Sufi poetry, and the dance as cosmology — keeping saint-miracles as faith, the origins and Salafi–Sufi debates open, and the popular de-Islamized 'universal Rumi' flagged as a modern distortion.

ch27.plateCaption: A dervish of the sema — the whirling ceremony of the Mevlevi — the right hand lifted to receive grace from heaven, the left turned down to pass it to the earth, the robe flaring as the soul turns toward union. An original geometric rendering, not a specific image.

ch28.title: Scholasticism
ch28.summary: The great medieval marriage of faith and reason. From Aquinas laying down his pen on the unfinished Summa ('all I have written seems like straw'), through the recovery of Aristotle via the Muslim commentators and the birth of the universities, the disputatio method and Abelard's Sic et Non, Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding' and ontological argument, Aquinas's Five Ways, and the later nominalist turn of Scotus and Ockham; with the parallel Jewish and Islamic projects (Maimonides, Avicenna, Averroes) and a symbology section on the four senses of Scripture and the Gothic cathedral as a 'summa in stone' — recording the great arguments as arguments still contested, not settled proofs, and correcting the 'Dark Ages' myth without overclaiming the reverse.
ch28.plateCaption: A Gothic rose window — order made visible, the “summa in stone”: a single figure in which every part is articulated and reconciled into a stable whole, as the schoolmen built their arguments. An original geometric rendering, not a specific window.

ch29.title: The Maya
ch29.summary: The rainforest civilization that built the only complete writing system in the ancient Americas and a religion of blood, maize, and precise time: the Popol Vuh and the Hero Twins of Xibalba, the pantheon of Itzamna and Chaak and Kukulkan, kingly bloodletting and the Vision Serpent, the calendars and the 2012 non-apocalypse, and the Sacred Cenote — with the archaeology kept distinct from conquest propaganda and modern myth.
ch29.plateCaption: A stepped temple-pyramid beneath the sun — the temple-mountain and solar kingship shared, independently, by the Maya, the Aztec, and the Inca. An original geometric rendering, not a specific monument.

ch30.title: Bhakti
ch30.summary: The devotional revolution of medieval India — a religion of passionate, personal love for God, sung in the mother tongue by weavers and washerwomen and untouchables, needing no priest, temple, or Sanskrit, only the heart. From the flowers under Kabir's shroud, through the Tamil Alvars and Nayanars, Ramanuja's philosophy of devotion, the saguna/nirguna divide, and the great company of saints (Basava and the Lingayats, Jnaneshwar and Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas); with a symbology section on the vernacular song, the divine name (nama-japa), Kabir's upside-down language, and the Lingayat ishtalinga — keeping the movement and its poetry distinct from the saints' hagiography, and meeting the Sufism of the same age. Closes the High Medieval era.
ch30.plateCaption: A lotus in bloom — the flower of devotion, rising from the water unstained: an emblem for a religion of love open to all. An original geometric rendering, not a specific image.

ch43.title: The Aztec
ch43.summary: The religion of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan: the cosmos of the Fifth Sun and the debt of blood, the pantheon of Tezcatlipoca, Quetzalcoatl, Huitzilopochtli, and Tlaloc, the Templo Mayor and the Coyolxauhqui stone, the calendars and the New Fire Ceremony, and the poetry of Nezahualcoyotl — with the reality of sacrifice held carefully apart from the conquerors' impossible numbers.

An original geometric rendering, not a copy of the monument.

ch44.title: The Inca
ch44.summary: The religion of the largest empire the Americas ever knew: the divine sun-emperor descended from Inti, the Coricancha and the ceque-wired sacred landscape, the royal mummies who still ruled, the capacocha children of the frozen peaks, and the knotted quipu — reconstructed from stone, cord, and the chronicles of the conquerors, with a steady eye on how much we can actually read.

ch56.title: Mandaeans, Yazidis & Druze
ch56.summary: The guarded faiths — three small, ancient, closed traditions of the Near East that the great monotheisms could neither absorb nor destroy. The Mandaeans, the last living Gnostics, who revere John the Baptist and reject Jesus, and baptize endlessly in living water; the Yazidis, whose Peacock Angel (Tawusi Melek) refused to bow to Adam — the source of the false ‘devil-worshipper’ libel and centuries of persecution, to the 2014 genocide; and the Druze, the esoteric 11th-century offshoot of Ismaili Islam venerating al-Hakim, teaching reincarnation and guarding secret Epistles of Wisdom, who accept no converts. A symbology of the Mandaean darfash and living water, the Yazidi peacock, and the Druze five-colored star — with the anti-Yazidi libel firmly refused and the guarded secrets respected.
ch56.plateCaption: Three emblems side by side: the five-pointed star of the Druze, whose five colours stand for five cosmic principles; the Mandaean darfash, a wooden cross-shaped standard draped in white silk and hung with myrtle (not a Christian cross); and a peacock feather for Tawûsî Melek, the Peacock Angel of the Yazidis. An original rendering, not a copy of any community’s objects.

ch59.title: Slavic & Baltic Paganism
ch59.summary: Europe’s last old gods — the Slavs Christianized by the 12th century, the Balts (Lithuania, 1387) the last pagan state on the continent. Perun the thunder-god thrown into the Dnieper at Kiev’s conversion; his opposite Veles the serpent of the underworld and their storm-versus-serpent myth; Vladimir’s 980 pantheon and the four-faced Svetovid of Arkona; the Baltic Dievas, Perkunas (whose name means oak), and the beloved sun-goddess Saule; sacred oak groves and the eternal fire; the ‘double faith’ and the folk survival, above all in the Latvian and Lithuanian dainos; and the modern revivals (Rodnovery, Romuva, Dievturiba). A symbology of the oak and thunder-mark, the eternal fire, and the four-faced idol — with the heavy reliance on hostile and reconstructed sources (and outright forgeries like the Book of Veles) flagged honestly.
ch59.plateCaption: The sacred oak of the thunder-god, a six-petalled “thunder-mark” of the kind carved on buildings as protection, and the eternal fire. An original composite; the pre-Christian meaning of such marks is partly reconstructed.

ch62.title: Native North American
ch62.summary: The sacred in all things — the vast, diverse, living religious world of Native North America (some 300 languages, no single religion). Cahokia and the mound-cities; the pervasive sacred power (Lakota Wakan Tanka, Algonquian Manitou, Iroquois orenda) and an animist cosmos; earth-diver and emergence creation and the trickster (Coyote, Raven, Nanabozho); the vision quest and the medicine person; the great ceremonies (Sun Dance, the sacred pipe of White Buffalo Calf Woman, potlatch, kachina, Green Corn); the monuments (Hopewell earthworks, Cahokia’s Monks Mound, Chaco’s astronomy) — with the racist ‘Mound Builder’ myth rejected; and the movements born of catastrophe (the Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee, the Longhouse religion, the peyote Native American Church). A symbology of the medicine wheel, the cross-in-circle and birdman, the sacred pipe, and the mound as world-axis.
ch62.plateCaption: A flat-topped earthen mound crowned by a building, after Monks Mound at Cahokia, with a circle of timber posts like the site’s “Woodhenge” and the sun above. A schematic drawing of archaeological monuments, not a sacred design.

ch72.title: The Cathars & Medieval Heresy
ch72.eraLabel: High Medieval · The Cathars & Medieval Heresy
ch72.summary: The good men and good women of Languedoc: two principles, souls as fallen angels, the consolamentum with the Gospel of John laid on the head, and the few Cathar texts the inquisitors missed; the Albigensian Crusade, Béziers and the pyre at Montségur; the inquisition and the Montaillou register; and the other dissenters, Waldensians, Marguerite Porete, the Spiritual Franciscans, Wyclif and Hus. With the great historians’ quarrel over whether the Cathar church was real or built by its persecutors, and the Grail legends and ‘Cathar castles’ sorted from the record.
ch72.plateCaption: An open book, the Gospel of John laid on the head in the consolamentum, above the peak of Montségur, where some two hundred good men and women were burned in 1244. An original, interpretive drawing; the Cathars left no emblem of their own.

ch81.title: Tengri & the Mongols
ch81.summary: The Eternal Blue Sky of the steppe peoples: Tengri in the Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions, Chinggis Khan on Burkhan Khaldun and the shaman Kököchü, the ‘by the power of Eternal Heaven’ formula on Mongol letters and seals, and a religious policy of tolerance that was pragmatism more than creed, as William of Rubruck’s 1254 debate at Karakorum shows. Then the khanates choose: Ghazan’s Islam in 1295, Kublai and the Tibetan lama Phagpa, Altan Khan’s title ‘Dalai Lama’ in 1578; the purges of 1937–39 and the post-1990 revival and neo-Tengrism. A symbology of the ovoo, khadag, sülde banner, milk libations, scapulimancy and the soyombo, with modern revival kept distinct from the medieval record.

v80.title: The Sefer Yetzirah
v80.dated: Date disputed: late antiquity to the early Islamic period; commented on by the 10th century
v80.held: Known from medieval manuscripts in three recensions
v80.summary: A very short Hebrew book describing creation through 'thirty-two wondrous paths': ten sefirot and the twenty-two letters, divided into three mothers, seven doubles and twelve simples and combined in 231 gates. Its date and setting are among the most disputed questions in Jewish studies.

v79.title: The Zohar, First Printings
v79.dated: Printed at Mantua and Cremona, 1558–1560; the Zohar itself first circulated in Castile in the 1280s
v79.held: Copies of the Mantua and Cremona editions in Jewish and national libraries
v79.summary: Kabbalah's great book was printed for the first time in two rival Italian editions, Mantua in three volumes and Cremona in one folio, over the protests of rabbis who thought secret lore should stay in manuscript. The Mantua pagination is still used to cite the Zohar today.

v19.title: The Book of Soyga
v19.held: Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS Bodley 908); British Library (Sloane MS 8)
v19.summary: John Dee's book of magic, ending in 36 grids of letters he could never read. An angel told him only Michael could explain it. Rediscovered in 1994; in 2006 a cryptographer showed the grids are generated from seed words by a fixed rule, not hidden messages.

v33.title: The Kartarpur Bir
v33.held: The Sodhi family, Kartarpur (Jalandhar district), Punjab
v33.summary: The volume that Sikh tradition holds is the first Adi Granth, compiled by Guru Arjan in 1604 with Bhai Gurdas as scribe. It was kept by a rival claimant to the Guruship, and scholars have seldom been allowed to see it. Its authority is revered, and its text history is debated.

v09.title: The Codex Gigas (“Devil's Bible”)
v09.summary: The largest surviving medieval manuscript (92 cm tall, about 75 kg), with a Bible, Josephus, Isidore, medicine, exorcisms, and a full-page devil facing the Heavenly City. Plundered from Prague in 1648 and thrown from a burning castle in 1697. The legend of the walled-up monk, and what the script says instead.

v06.title: The Crown of Thorns
v06.dated: Documented from 1238 (Paris); earlier history by tradition; never dated
v06.held: Notre-Dame de Paris (axial chapel, reliquary of 2024)
v06.summary: A ring of bundled rushes bound with gold thread, with no thorns left on it, for which Saint Louis paid almost half his annual revenue and built the Sainte-Chapelle. Traced from the Gospel mockery through Constantinople, Venice and the Revolution to the night Notre-Dame burned.

v01.title: The Voynich Manuscript
v01.held: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University — MS 408
v01.summary: A fifteenth-century vellum book in an unknown script that no one has been able to read — radiocarbon-dated, its owners traced from Rudolf II's Prague, and every proposed 'solution' tested and found wanting. Study all of Yale's page scans at full resolution, load the standard transliteration, and test a decipherment of your own.

v03.title: The Emerald Tablet
v03.held: No physical tablet is known — the text survives in Arabic & Latin sources
v03.summary: Fourteen lines that became the scripture of European alchemy — 'that which is below is like that which is above.' Traced from the Arabic Book of the Secret of Creation to Newton's own translation, with the Latin and a line-by-line working translation, and kept apart from Doreal's 20th-century 'Tablets of Thoth.'

v24.title: The Sudarium of Oviedo
v24.summary: A stained linen face-cloth, venerated as the sudarium of John 20:7 and shown three times a year. Documented from the opening of the Arca Santa in 1075, radiocarbon-dated to around the seventh century, and claimed to match the Shroud.

v31.title: The Dresden Codex
v31.dated: Usually dated 11th–14th century; the date is debated
v31.held: SLUB Dresden (Saxon State and University Library), Mscr.Dresd.R.310
v31.summary: The finest of the four Maya books that survived the Spanish conquest: a folding screen of bark paper, bought in Vienna in 1739 and damaged by water in 1945. Its tables track Venus, predict eclipse seasons, and bind both to the sacred 260-day count.

v32.title: The Popol Vuh Manuscript
v32.dated: Copied c. 1700–1715 by Francisco Ximénez; the lost K'iche' original c. 1550s
v32.summary: The K'iche' Maya book of creation, the Hero Twins and the lords of Xibalba, which survives only because a Dominican friar in Chichicastenango copied it around 1701, K'iche' beside Spanish. The alphabetic original, written by K'iche' nobles after the conquest, is lost.

v41.title: The Codex Borgia
v41.dated: Late 15th or early 16th century, central Mexico
v41.summary: A painted screenfold of deerskin from the Puebla–Tlaxcala region of Mexico, among the very few divinatory books to survive the conquest. It is a manual of the 260-day count, with gods, omens, a Venus almanac and a mysterious central section that may describe a journey through the night.

v83.title: The Codex Boturini
v83.dated: Shortly before or after the Spanish conquest; c. 1520s–1540s
v83.held: Biblioteca Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Mexico City
v83.summary: The 'Strip of the Pilgrimage', a 5.5-metre amate screenfold drawn in black and never coloured, telling the Mexica migration from Aztlan in footprints, place glyphs and year counts. It breaks off mid-story, during the war of Colhuacan against Xochimilco.

v13.title: The Tilma of Guadalupe
v13.dated: Devotion attested by 1556; tradition dates the image to 1531
v13.held: Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, Mexico City
v13.summary: The cloak venerated as Juan Diego's, bearing the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe. It was attacked in 1556 as 'painted by an Indian, Marcos', survived a bomb in 1921, and was studied in infrared in 1979. The Nahuatl account, the documents, the science and the myths, kept apart.

v51.title: The Codex Mendoza
v51.held: Bodleian Library, Oxford (MS. Arch. Selden. A. 1)
v51.summary: Painted by Nahua artists for the first viceroy of New Spain, with Spanish notes: the founding of Tenochtitlan, the tribute of the empire, and an Aztec life from birth to old age. Bound for the emperor Charles V, it was seized by French privateers and ended up in Oxford.

v65.title: The Staff God of Tiwanaku
v65.dated: Tiwanaku flourished c. 500–1000 CE; the gateway's exact date is uncertain
v65.held: In place: Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, Bolivia (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
v65.summary: A monolithic gateway of andesite at Tiwanaku, carved with a frontal figure holding two staffs, its head ringed with rays, flanked by rows of winged attendants. The figure belongs to a 'Staff God' tradition running through Andean art for two thousand years. Later writers linked it to the Inca creator Viracocha.

v62.title: The Inca Khipu
v62.dated: Mostly c. 1400–1600 CE; earlier Wari examples c. 600–1000 CE
v62.held: About 1,000 or more in museums worldwide (Lima, Berlin, New York, Harvard and elsewhere)
v62.summary: Bundles of knotted cords that ran the largest empire of the Americas without an alphabet: census counts, tribute, calendars, and, the Spanish said, histories. The numbers were cracked in 1912. Whether some khipus also recorded words remains one of the great open questions of decipherment.

v87.title: The Diwan Abatur
v87.dated: The published copy DC 8 is 18th-century; the text is older, date uncertain
v87.held: Bodleian Library, Oxford (Drower Collection, DC 8); Vatican Library (Borgiani Siriaci 175)
v87.summary: A Mandaean illustrated scroll over six metres long that maps the soul's road after death through the maṭarātā, or watch-houses, across the river Hitpun in the ship Shahrat, to Abatur, who weighs it. Published in English by E. S. Drower in 1950.

v67.title: The Aramaic Incantation Bowls
v67.held: About 2,000 or more in museums and private collections (Penn Museum, British Museum, Schøyen Collection and others)
v67.summary: Clay bowls written with spells in a spiral, sometimes around a drawing of a chained demon, and buried upside down under houses to trap evil. Made for Jewish, Christian, Mandaean and pagan clients in Babylonia, they are the everyday magic of the world that produced the Babylonian Talmud.

metatron.name: Metatron
metatron.desc: Great angel of the Hebrew Book of Enoch (3 Enoch), identified there with the transformed Enoch, and an important figure in Jewish mysticism.

lilith.name: Lilith
lilith.desc: A demoness who threatens women and infants in Jewish tradition, named once in Isaiah 34:14 and bound on the Babylonian incantation bowls.
lilith.contested: The story that she was Adam's first wife comes from the medieval Alphabet of Ben Sira, not from the Bible.

ezekiel.name: Ezekiel
ezekiel.desc: Prophet of the Babylonian exile who sees the throne-chariot of God, with its wheels full of eyes, and the valley of dry bones restored to life. His vision became the root of Merkavah mysticism.

muhammad.name: Muhammad
muhammad.desc: The Prophet of Islam (c. 570–632 CE), who received the revelations of the Qur'an in Mecca and Medina and founded the first Muslim community. Muslims hold him to be the last of the prophets, the 'Seal of the Prophets'. Following Islamic practice, he is shown only by his name in calligraphy.

ali.name: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
ali.desc: Cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, fourth caliph in Sunni reckoning and first Imam of Shiʿi Islam, assassinated at Kufa in 661.
